import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 137

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/137](https://www.erdosproblems.com/137)
-/

namespace Erdos137

/--
Let $k\geq 3$. Can the product of any $k$ consecutive integers $N$ ever be powerful? That is,
must there always exist a prime $p\mid N$ such that $p^2\nmid N$?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_137 : answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ k ≥ 3, ∀ n, ¬ (∏ x ∈ Finset.Ioc n (n + k), x).Powerful := by
  sorry

/--
Let $k\geq 2$. Erdős and Selfridge [ES75] proved that the product of any $k$ consecutive
integers $N$ cannot be a perfect power.

[ES75] P. Erdös, J. L. Selfridge, "The product of consecutive integers is never a power",
  Illinois J. Math. 19(2): 292-301, 1975
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_137.variants.perfect_power (k : ℕ) (hk : k ≥ 2) (n : ℕ) (x l : ℕ) (hl : 2 ≤ l) :
    (∏ x ∈ Finset.Ioc n (n + k), x) ≠ x ^ l := by
  sorry

/--
Erdős [Er82c] conjectures that, if $k$ is fixed, then for all $n$ sufficiently large and all
positive integers $m$, there must be at least $k$ distinct primes $p$ such that
$p\mid m(m+1)\cdots (m+n)$ and yet $p^2$ does not divide the right hand side.

[Er82c] Erdős, Paul, "Miscellaneous problems in number theory". Congr. Numer. (1982), 25-45.,
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_137.variants.multiple_powerful_factors (k : ℕ) : ∀ᶠ n in Filter.atTop,
    ∀ (m : ℕ) (hm : 0 < m),
    letI N := ∏ x ∈ Finset.Ioc m (m + n), x
    ∃ P : Finset ℕ, P.card = k ∧ ∀ p ∈ P, p.Prime ∧
    p ∣ N ∧ ¬ p ^ 2 ∣ N := by
  sorry

end Erdos137

reformulations.difference: Lean uses the product (m+1)⋯(m+n), whereas the source uses m⋯(m+n). It also asks for a chosen finite set of exactly k qualifying primes rather than saying “at least k distinct primes.”
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Suppose the Lean assertion holds for all n ≥ T. For a source interval starting at m ≥ 2, use Lean parameters (m−1,n+1). For m=1, use (1,n): omitting the factor 1 leaves the product unchanged. Thus the source assertion holds with threshold T. Conversely, if the source assertion holds for all n ≥ S, then for a Lean interval with n ≥ S+1 use source parameters (m+1,n−1). These changes preserve uniformity in m. Finally, existence of a chosen k-element set is equivalent to having at least k qualifying primes, since any larger finite witness can be restricted to a k-element subset. The full equivalence was proved as Review137.multiple_variant_equiv in /workspace/review/scratch.lean, without sorry or reliance on the conjecture declarations.

sources_consulted: P. Erdős and J. L. Selfridge, The product of consecutive integers is never a power, Illinois J. Math. 19 (1975), 292–301, especially the introduction and Theorem 1. https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1975-46.pdf (read via Jina text extraction).

P. Erdős, Miscellaneous problems in number theory, Congr. Numer. 34 (1982), 25–45, especially pp. 27–28, equations (5)–(6) and the accompanying conjectures. https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1982-08.pdf (read via Jina text extraction).
review.notes: Checked all three declarations. The 1975 primary paper explicitly states k ≥ 2, exponent ≥ 2, and n ≥ 0, matching perfect_power despite the website summary mentioning only k ≥ 3. The source still records Problem 137 as open and presents the stronger variant as a conjecture. Checked Nat.Powerful and its prime-factor semantics, including 0 and 1; proved the prime-witness characterization and positivity of the interval products. The scratch file compiles successfully and includes boundary checks and finite computational tests. No mathematical defects or status discrepancies were found.
